doc.title: Bill Huntington and Charlie Suhor Interview, 1992-04-06

title: Suhor on Huntington's roots among older black players
summary: Suhor praises Huntington's deep traditional roots; Huntington says older black players embodied what he wanted to hear, with a reaction against white music.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: So, before you get too far into your bass stuff, I wanted to pick up on something you said about your lack of a peer group when you were with Lawrence Marrero and the black musicians. That was one thing that I think is very unique about you, the fact that of all the players like myself and others who came up with Dixieland as our love, we just didn't have that deep connection with the early traditional players. And it's easier conceptually to pick up the fluff aspects of Dixieland. It's very difficult, it sounds decent, it sounds okay, it's very difficult to pick up the core of the stuff in the New Orleans tradition. And you were unique among us in having that kind of a rootsy connection. And before I knew anything other than your name and you were going to sit in on guitar, and that sounded like a drag to me on a gig once with Buddy Prima. This guitar player comes in, he's setting up and he's playing, and I said, well, guitar players usually get in the way. I said, we're grooving along, and Bill plays the first lick. I said, that is jazz. That's the conception. That's what it is. And later I found out how deep his roots were in it. So I think that's a part of your conception, and it's a part of a unique, fairly unique in the white community in terms of having bridged so many eras in jazz and having had those genuine roots that are so intense. And I value that, and I'd say that if you weren't here, so I wanted to say it now before it got away from me.
Yeah, well, thanks. You know, I don't really know why it happened except that, to me, the older black players embodied what I wanted to hear.

You know, and like I said, it did affect me socially and it affected me psychologically in the sense that for a long time I developed this kind of reaction formation against white music. And I think it's very ironic that as a child I felt this way, and I can see it in so many white people today, which is unfortunate.
